legend.name: Mesosaurus fossils
legend.meaning: Where the reptile's fossils are found

note.text: Look at South America's east coast, with its bulge sticking out into the Atlantic.
Africa's west coast curves in where South America's bulges out, like puzzle pieces.

steps.title: Fossils
steps.instruction: Trace the two areas where Mesosaurus fossils are found.

note.text: Mesosaurus was a small freshwater reptile. Its fossils are found in both South America and Africa, but it couldn't cross an ocean.

steps.title: Ridge
steps.instruction: Trace the ridge down the middle of the Atlantic.

note.text: Down the middle of the ocean runs a ridge where plates pull apart and new sea floor forms.

steps.title: Moving apart
steps.instruction: Draw the arrows showing the continents moving apart.

note.text: The continents still drift apart, about 2.5 cm a year: roughly as fast as your fingernails grow.

steps.title: Explain the fossils
steps.question: How did the same freshwater reptile end up on two continents an ocean apart?

options.text: The continents were joined when it lived, and later drifted apart
options.feedback: Yes. Alfred Wegener used fossils like these as evidence for a supercontinent, which he named Pangaea (also spelled Pangea).
Mesosaurus lived in fresh water and couldn't cross a whole ocean.

options.text: Two different animals evolved to look the same
options.feedback: The fossils match, and so do the rocks around them. The simpler answer: the land was joined.
The fossils are buried in rock millions of years old, long before people.

steps.title: More evidence
steps.question: Which other finding supports the idea that the continents were once joined?

options.text: Matching rock layers on the two coasts
options.feedback: Right. Wegener found rock layers in Brazil matching those in Africa, and mountains in Canada matching ones in Britain.
Every continent has rivers, so that's no evidence they were joined.
Weather changes over time and doesn't show the land was joined.
People came much later. Matching rocks and fossils are the evidence.

steps.title: The missing piece
steps.question: Why did most geologists reject Wegener's idea at first, around 1912?

options.text: He couldn't explain what force could move whole continents
options.feedback: Yes. Decades later, sea-floor spreading and plate tectonics supplied the mechanism, and his idea was accepted.

options.text: The coasts didn't fit at all
options.feedback: The fit was striking. The real problem was that he had no mechanism for the movement.
He used fossils as evidence. What he lacked was a force to move the continents.
Good maps existed. The missing piece was a force to move continents.
